200: From the earliest post-apostolic writers onward, the church insisted that the dead would be raised in the flesh, not merely survive as souls. Against Greek philosophical contempt for the body and against Gnostic teachers who denied the resurrection of the flesh, writers argued from creation, from nature's cycles, from God's power and justice, and above all from Christ's own resurrection.
207:
1 Clement (c. 96) argues for the resurrection from day following night, seed dying and growing, and the legend of the phoenix (chs 24-26), a sign of how naturally early Christians reached for analogies in nature. Justin (c. 155) defends the possibility of resurrection by comparing it with the formation of a human from a tiny seed (*1 Apology* 18-19).

The treatise *On the Resurrection* traditionally ascribed to Athenagoras (c. 180) gives a philosophical case: humans are made as body-soul unities for an everlasting purpose, and divine justice requires that the whole person, who acted in the body, be judged. Its authenticity is debated (R. M. Grant and others have argued for a later date or different author).

Irenaeus (c. 180) argued against Gnostics that the flesh which God formed and which the Eucharist nourishes is capable of incorruption (*Against Heresies* 5.2-3). Tertullian's *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* (c. 208-212) is the fullest Latin defence, insisting on the identity of the risen flesh. Later, Origen proposed that the risen body retains a 'form' (eidos) while its matter changes; Methodius of Olympus (*On the Resurrection*) attacked this as compromising material identity. The phrase 'resurrection of the flesh' (carnis resurrectionem) entered the Old Roman Creed and the Apostles' Creed.

Shift: the doctrine remained creedal everywhere, but emphasis moved over the centuries toward the fate of the soul at death (see 'going-to-heaven-shift'). Bynum shows, however, that medieval Western thinkers continued to care intensely about bodily identity and resurrection.
209: Irenaeus taught that the final hope is not escape from the material world but its renewal: the righteous will reign on a restored earth, creation itself will be freed and made fruitful, and then the whole cosmos will be transfigured. For him salvation is the healing and fulfilment of creation (recapitulation in Christ), against Gnostics who despised matter.
210:
In *Against Heresies* 5.32-36 Irenaeus argues that it is fitting for the righteous to receive the reward of their sufferings in the same creation in which they suffered. He insists that the promises to Abraham of the land must be literally fulfilled, that Isaiah's prophecies of peaceable animals and abundance are not merely allegorical (5.33-35), and that 'neither the substance nor the matter of the creation' is annihilated, only its 'fashion' passes away (5.36.1, reading 1 Cor 7:31). He ties this to his chiliasm (see 'chiliasm').

Shift: as chiliasm declined and Platonist spirituality grew, the renewal of the material cosmos received less attention in Western theology, though it was never denied in principle (Aquinas affirms a renewal of the world after judgment). Twentieth-century theology (Moltmann, Wright, Middleton, and much Reformed 'new creation' theology) has revived Irenaeus as a key witness. Critics caution that some revivals underplay the discontinuity and the transfiguring, God-centred character of the final state stressed by other Fathers.
211: Hades as waiting place: the intermediate state
212: Many second- and third-century writers taught that ordinary souls do not go straight to heaven at death but wait in Hades (the underworld), divided into places of refreshment and of distress, until the resurrection. Martyrs were often an exception, entering paradise immediately.
216:
Irenaeus argued that, as Christ went into the place of the dead for three days before rising, so his disciples' souls go to an invisible place appointed by God and await the resurrection there (*Against Heresies* 5.31.2); he regarded the view that souls go straight to heaven as a Gnostic error. Justin similarly criticizes those who say souls are taken up to heaven at death (*Dialogue* 80; the precise wording should be checked).

Tertullian (*On the Soul* 55) located all souls in the underworld except the martyrs, who go at once to paradise (citing the souls under the altar, Rev 6:9). He also suggests that souls already experience a foretaste of reward or punishment in Hades (ch. 58). A Greek fragment titled *Against Plato, On the Cause of the Universe*, attributed to Hippolytus (sometimes to Josephus in manuscripts), describes Hades as a subterranean region with a bright region (the 'bosom of Abraham') for the righteous and a region near the lake of fire for the wicked, awaiting judgment; its authorship is disputed.

Shift: by the fourth and fifth centuries the dominant expectation was that the souls of the holy enter the presence of Christ at death (Cyprian already expressed this for martyrs and the faithful; Augustine discusses 'secret receptacles' for souls, *Enchiridion* 109). In the West this developed into heaven, hell and purgatory as immediate destinations, defined in 1336 (see 'beatific-vision'); in the East the interim state remained less defined, with prayer for the departed.
218: Early Christians widely believed that between his death and resurrection Christ went to the realm of the dead, proclaimed victory, and freed the righteous of the old covenant. The idea appears in Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Melito and later in the *Gospel of Nicodemus*, and entered the Apostles' Creed as 'he descended into hell'. Its biblical basis and meaning remain debated.
224:
Ignatius says the prophets awaited Christ as their teacher and that on his coming he raised them from the dead (*Magnesians* 9). Justin accuses Jews of removing from Jeremiah a passage about the Lord remembering his dead who slept and going down to preach salvation to them (*Dialogue* 72); the same saying is quoted by Irenaeus. Irenaeus also reports an elder's teaching that the Lord descended to the regions beneath the earth announcing his advent (*Against Heresies* 4.27.2). Melito's *Peri Pascha* pictures Christ trampling death and binding the strong one.

The *Gospel of Nicodemus* (a Latin and Greek work whose descent section is usually dated fourth to sixth century) dramatizes the 'Harrowing of Hell': Christ breaks the gates, binds Satan, and leads Adam and the patriarchs out. This shaped medieval drama and Eastern Anastasis icons. The creedal phrase descendit ad inferna (later ad inferos) is first attested in the fourth century (the Fourth Formula of Sirmium, 359, and the Aquileian creed reported by Rufinus) and entered the received Apostles' Creed.

Interpretation varied: (1) a proclamation of victory and liberation of Old Testament saints (patristic mainstream, Catholic, Orthodox); (2) Christ suffering the torments of hell on the cross in soul (Calvin, *Institutes* 2.16.10); (3) simply that Christ truly died and was buried, entering the state of death (many Reformed, the Westminster Larger Catechism 50); (4) some evangelicals (e.g. Grudem) argue the phrase should be dropped. 1 Pet 3:19 is itself debated: preaching to the dead, to imprisoned fallen angels (the Watchers of 1 Enoch), or through Noah to his contemporaries (Augustine's reading).
226: Many influential second-century Christians in Asia Minor and beyond expected that after the resurrection of the righteous Christ would reign for a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem on a fruitful, renewed earth, before the final judgment. This 'chiliasm' (from Greek chilioi, thousand) or 'millenarianism' is attested in Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Hippolytus, Lactantius and others.
231:
Papias (early second century) passed on, according to Irenaeus, a saying traced through 'the elders who saw John' of vines with ten thousand branches and enormous yields in the kingdom (*Against Heresies* 5.33.3-4). Eusebius records that Papias taught a corporeal thousand-year reign after the resurrection and judges him a man of 'very small intelligence', blaming him for passing the view to Irenaeus and others (*Ecclesiastical History* 3.39.12-13).

Justin (*Dialogue* 80-81) says he and other fully orthodox Christians expect a resurrection of the flesh and a thousand years in a rebuilt and enlarged Jerusalem, citing Isaiah 65 and Revelation 20; he also admits that many Christians of pure and pious faith do not share this view. Irenaeus defends it at length (5.32-36). Tertullian (*Against Marcion* 3.24) describes a thousand-year reign in a Jerusalem let down from heaven.

Scholarly debate: older accounts treated chiliasm as the near-universal second-century view. Charles E. Hill argued that non-chiliastic eschatology (with the righteous going to heaven at death) was also widespread and early, so the picture was mixed. Modern premillennialists claim continuity with these Fathers; amillennialists note that the early chiliasts did not hold dispensational features such as a pretribulation rapture.
233: From the third century, especially in Alexandria and later in the Latin West through Augustine, the literal thousand-year kingdom was increasingly criticized as carnal and Jewish-sounding, and Revelation 20 was reread spiritually as the present reign of Christ with his saints. By the fifth century chiliasm had become a minority or suspect view in both East and West.
240:
Origen rejected those who expected bodily pleasures, eating, drinking and marriage in the promised kingdom, interpreting the prophecies spiritually (*On First Principles* 2.11.2). Around 250-260 Dionysius of Alexandria, Origen's pupil, met the chiliasm of the Egyptian bishop Nepos, who had written a *Refutation of the Allegorists*. Dionysius debated his followers for three days in the Arsinoe district and, according to his own account preserved by Eusebius (*HE* 7.24), persuaded them; he also argued on stylistic grounds that Revelation was not written by the author of the Fourth Gospel (7.25). Eusebius himself dismissed Papias's views (3.39) and was cool toward Revelation.

In the West, the Donatist Tyconius (c. 380) read Revelation as a description of the church's ongoing struggle. Augustine, who admits he once held a spiritualized form of chiliasm, rejected the carnal version and interpreted the thousand years as the whole period of the church between Christ's first and second comings, with the first resurrection as spiritual regeneration (*City of God* 20.7-9). This became the dominant Western reading for over a millennium (amillennialism, in modern terms).

Causes proposed by historians: Alexandrian allegorical exegesis; the end of persecution under Constantine, making the church's present reign seem plausible; reaction against Montanist prophecy; anti-Jewish polemic; and doubts over Revelation's canonicity in the East. Chiliasm was never condemned by an ecumenical council, and revived in various forms (Joachim of Fiore's influence, radical Reformation, seventeenth-century Puritans, and modern premillennialism). The Augsburg Confession (art. 17) rejected 'Jewish opinions' of an earthly kingdom before the resurrection.
242: The dominant early and later view held that the impenitent wicked would suffer conscious, everlasting punishment in fire after the judgment. It appears in 2 Clement, Ignatius, the Martyrdom of Polycarp, Justin, Athenagoras, Tertullian and Minucius Felix, and receives its classic defence in Augustine, *City of God* book 21.
246:
2 Clement (mid-second century) warns that the ungodly will be punished with terrible torments in unquenchable fire (17.5-7, drawing on Isa 66:24). The Martyrdom of Polycarp contrasts the brief fire of the persecutor with the fire of coming judgment and eternal punishment (11.2). Justin tells the emperor that each person goes to eternal punishment or salvation according to their deeds, and that this punishment lasts not a thousand years, as Plato said, but an eternal period (*1 Apology* 8). Tertullian and Minucius Felix (*Octavius* 35) describe a fire that torments without consuming.

Augustine's *City of God* book 21 is the most influential defence: he argues that bodies can burn without being consumed (21.2-7), answers the 'merciful' who hope for limited punishment (21.17-27), and insists that 'eternal' must mean the same for punishment and life in Matt 25:46 (21.23). He notes that in his day very many (Enchiridion 112) pitied the damned and doubted endless punishment, showing the question was live.

Shift: this became the official teaching of the Western church (e.g. Fourth Lateran 1215) and of Orthodoxy, and was retained by the Reformers. Since the nineteenth century, increasing numbers of Protestants have adopted conditional immortality or hopeful universalism; defenders argue that eternal punishment best fits Jesus' teaching and the seriousness of sin against an infinite God, and critics argue it misreads 'destruction' language and portrays God as retributive without end.
248: Several early writers taught that the soul is not immortal by nature but receives continued existence from God, who grants immortality to the righteous. Some modern annihilationists read them as early witnesses that the wicked eventually cease to exist; other scholars argue these writers still held to everlasting punishment, and only Arnobius clearly taught annihilation.
251:
In the *Dialogue* (chs 5-6) Justin, recounting his conversion conversation with an old man, rejects the Platonic claim that souls are naturally immortal: souls live because God wills them to live and could cease if he did not; the souls of the unrighteous are punished 'as long as God wills them to exist and be punished'. Whether Justin envisaged an end to their existence is disputed, because elsewhere he speaks of eternal punishment (*1 Apology* 8). The exact wording should be checked against a critical edition.

Theophilus of Antioch (*To Autolycus* 2.27) says humans were made neither mortal nor immortal by nature, but capable of either, depending on obedience. Irenaeus (*Against Heresies* 2.34.3) says souls continue to exist because God grants it, and that those who are ungrateful deprive themselves of 'length of days for ever and ever'; conditionalists cite this, while others note Irenaeus also describes eternal punishment (e.g. 4.28.2, 5.27.2).

Arnobius of Sicca (c. 300), a recent convert writing against pagans, is the clearest early annihilationist: souls are of a 'middle quality' and, if they do not know God, are finally consumed and pass into nothingness (*Against the Heathen* 2.14). His theology was idiosyncratic and little followed.

Shift: after Augustine, the natural immortality of the soul became standard (defined at the Fifth Lateran Council, 1513). Conditional immortality revived among some Socinians and English dissenters, in nineteenth-century writers such as Edward White, among Seventh-day Adventists and Christadelphians, and among twentieth-century evangelicals (John Stott tentatively, Edward Fudge, Clark Pinnock).
252: Apokatastasis: the hope of universal restoration
253: A significant line of Greek-speaking theologians held that punishment after death is remedial and that God will finally restore all rational creatures, possibly including the devil, to union with himself. Origen is its most famous proponent; Gregory of Nyssa gave it a refined form; Didymus the Blind, Evagrius and, in the Syriac tradition, Isaac of Nineveh express related hopes. Clement of Alexandria's position is debated.
259:
Clement of Alexandria described divine punishments as educative and corrective (e.g. *Stromata* 7.2), though whether he expected all to be saved is disputed. Origen (*On First Principles* 1.6) argued that the end will be like the beginning: through long ages of discipline all rational beings will be brought back, so that God will be 'all in all' (1 Cor 15:28). He treated this as a theological exploration, at times hedging (whether the devil would be saved, and whether souls might fall again, are contested points in his texts, transmitted partly through Rufinus's softened Latin).

Gregory of Nyssa, a revered Nicene bishop, taught in *On the Soul and the Resurrection* and the *Catechetical Oration* (26) that the purifying fire will remove evil from every creature, since evil is finite and non-being, so that finally even the inventor of evil will be healed. Didymus the Blind and Evagrius continued the Origenist tradition. Isaac of Nineveh (seventh century), revered in East and West Syriac and Greek Orthodox monasticism, argued in his recently recovered Second Part that God's love makes Gehenna a temporary scourge of love and that God would not create beings he knew would be lost forever (specific discourse numbers to be checked).

Assessment is contested. Ramelli argues apokatastasis was widely held, rooted in Scripture and compatible with orthodoxy; McClymond and others argue it depends on Platonist metaphysics, was always a minority, and was rightly rejected. Augustine opposed it, and the Origenist form was condemned in the sixth century (see 'condemnations-543-553'). Modern defenders include Sergius Bulgakov, Hans Urs von Balthasar (as a hope, not a certainty) and David Bentley Hart.
261: In 543 the emperor Justinian issued an edict, with anathemas confirmed by a home synod in Constantinople, condemning Origenist doctrines including the pre-existence of souls and the temporary character of punishment. In 553, around the Fifth Ecumenical Council (Constantinople II), fifteen anathemas against Origenist teachings were adopted. Whether these were formally acts of the ecumenical council, and whether they target Origen himself, Gregory of Nyssa's hope, or a specific sixth-century monastic Origenism, is debated.
268:
Disputes among Palestinian monks over Origenist teachings (pre-existence of souls, a spherical resurrection body, the restoration of demons, and the Evagrian Christology of the 'isochristoi') prompted imperial intervention. Justinian's 543 edict to Patriarch Menas listed anathemas, including one against anyone who says the punishment of demons or impious humans is temporary and will end. The 553 anathemas, preserved separately from the main council acts, target a cosmology closely linked to Evagrius more than Origen's own words.

Debated points: (1) Were the fifteen anathemas passed at the ecumenical council itself? Many scholars (e.g. Richard Price, following earlier research) think they were approved by the assembled bishops shortly before the formal opening, giving them conciliar weight in practice; others argue they lack strict ecumenical status. (2) Canon 11 includes Origen's name in a list of heretics; some scholars have suggested the name was a later insertion, though most accept it. (3) Gregory of Nyssa was never condemned and remains a saint, which some take to mean that his version of the hope (without pre-existence) was not the target; others read the 543 anathema as rejecting all temporary-hell views.

Effect: after the sixth century, universal restoration as a doctrine was regarded as heretical in both East and West, though it continued in some Syriac writers (Isaac of Nineveh, Stephen bar Sudaili earlier), in Eriugena, and resurfaced in modern theology.
269: Early prayer and offerings for the dead
270: From at least the late second century Christians commemorated and prayed for the departed, offered the Eucharist on the anniversaries of their deaths, and inscribed requests for refreshment (refrigerium) and peace on tombs. This practice, shared by East and West, is the root from which both Orthodox prayer for the departed and the Latin doctrine of purgatory grew.
274:
Tertullian lists annual offerings for the dead as an established custom (*De corona* 3) and says a widow prays for her husband's soul and seeks refreshment for him (*On Monogamy* 10). In the *Passion of Perpetua*, Perpetua prays for her dead young brother Dinocrates and sees him moved from a place of thirst and suffering to refreshment (7-8). Inscriptions in the Roman catacombs ask peace and refreshment for the departed. The Jerusalem *Mystagogical Catecheses* (5.9-10) describe prayer for the departed in the Eucharistic anaphora. Augustine asks readers to remember his mother Monica at the altar (*Confessions* 9.13).

The Jewish precedent of 2 Maccabees 12:39-45 (Judas's offering for the fallen) was cited, though this book is outside the Protestant canon. Protestants often cite 2 Tim 1:16-18 as a possible but uncertain instance (Paul's prayer for Onesiphorus, who may have died).

Shift: these practices did not by themselves imply a defined place of purifying punishment; they expressed communion and hope. The Orthodox continue prayer for the departed without a doctrine of purgatory; the Latin West developed purgatory (see 'purgatory-development'); the Reformers generally abolished prayers for the dead as lacking scriptural warrant (Anglican practice later varied).
276: The Western church gradually defined a post-death purification for those who die in God's grace but not yet fully purified. Seeds appear in Augustine; Gregory the Great's *Dialogues* popularized purgatorial fire for lesser sins; the noun purgatorium emerges in the twelfth century; the Councils of Lyon II (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563) defined it. The Orthodox reject the Latin form (especially material fire and satisfaction) while praying for the dead, and the Reformers rejected it outright.
